parole.testo: Borrowed from Hokkien 田草 (chhân-chháu, “grass jelly”) / 仙草 (sian-chháu / chhian-chháu / chhan-chháu / chhin-chháu, “grass jelly”). Compare Hiligaynon sansaw.

Borrowed from Hokkien, possibly 看好 (khòaⁿ-hó) or 看護 /看护 (khàn-hō͘ / khòaⁿ-hō͘ / khan-hō͘) or 看虎 (khòaⁿ hó͘, literally “watching the tiger”). Compare Tagalog kuwaho, Kapampangan kuwaho, English Cuajo, English Khanhoo.

parole.significato: a sweet pastry historically made by Chinese people
parole.testo: Borrowed from Hokkien [Term?]. See also Early Manila Hokkien 香餅 /香饼 (hioⁿ-piáⁿ, literally “fragrant pastry”), Indonesian bakpia.
From Hokkien 荔枝 (lē-chi) + -a or Hokkien 荔枝仔 (lē-chi-á). Doublet of lichi. See also Portuguese lichia.
Borrowed from Hokkien 荔枝 (lē-chi). Doublet of lechía. See also Portuguese lichia.

Borrowed from Hokkien, either: * 扁食 (pán-si̍t, “wonton dumpling”, literally “flattened food; flat and thin food”), according to Manuel (1948), which he described as “[pán(cook rice to make noodle)-sit(food, meal), meat-balls sautéd with noodle.]”. parole.significato: fish sauce (a fish or shrimp brine byproduct from making bagoong, used as an ingredient or condiment in the Philippines)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Hokkien 膎汁 (kê-chiap, “fish sauce”, literally “pickled fish juice”). Compare Tagalog ketsap, Kapampangan kesiap.
From Hokkien 茶 (tê). Doublet of cha. Compare Dutch thee.
